lead: Both readings today are about foundations. Paul tells the Colossians to live “rooted and built up” in Christ, in whom “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily”, and not to be carried off by teachings that do not come from him. Jesus ends the Sermon on the Plain with two houses: one built on rock by someone who hears his words and acts on them, the other built without a foundation. The key words are rooted and doing.

r.h: Rooted and built up in him
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. The church there was founded not by Paul but by his co-worker Epaphras (1:7). The letter warns against a teaching that called itself “philosophy” and mixed reverence for the “elemental spirits”, special festivals, food rules and the worship of angels (2:8, 16–18). Paul's answer is Christ: in him the Colossians already have everything.

The letter presents itself as written by Paul from prison. Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in Paul's name, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.
str: vv. 6–7: continue to live in Christ, as you were taught.
v. 8: a warning against empty philosophy.
vv. 9–10: the fullness of God dwells in Christ, and you are filled in him.
vv. 11–12: the circumcision of Christ: buried and raised with him in Baptism.
vv. 13–15: God forgave us, cancelled the record against us, and triumphed over the powers.
kw: The phrase is debated. It can mean the basic elements of the world, or the first principles of a teaching, or spiritual powers thought to rule the world. In every case Paul's point is the same: nothing in creation can take the place of Christ.
God's whole being and life. It does not dwell in Christ partly or for a time, but “bodily”, really and permanently, in the Word made flesh.
A handwritten note of debt, signed by the debtor. Our sins had made us debtors before God; God has wiped out the bond and nailed it to the cross.
vv: As you therefore have received Christ Jesus the Lord, continue to live your lives in him,
“Received” is the word for receiving a tradition that is handed on. The Colossians did not receive only teaching about Christ; they received Christ himself.
For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,
One of the clearest statements of the divinity of Christ in the New Testament. The Church has always read it with the faith of the Councils: Christ is true God and true man in one person.
when you were buried with him in baptism, you were also raised with him through faith in the power of God,
Baptism is not a symbol of something done elsewhere. In it the believer is joined to the death and resurrection of Christ.
erasing the record that stood against us with its legal demands. He set this aside, nailing it to the cross.
The picture is bold: the note of our debt is nailed up beside the Crucified, cancelled. What condemned us has been taken away.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Baptism signifies and brings about the Christian's descent into the tomb with Christ, dying to sin in order to walk in newness of life (CCC 628; Colossians 2:12). It also sees in the circumcision of Jesus a sign that prefigures the “circumcision of Christ”, which is Baptism (CCC 527). Paul's warning against empty philosophy does not condemn reason, which the Church honours; it warns against any system that would put something other than Christ at the centre.

set: These verses close the Sermon on the Plain (6:20–49), Luke's shorter form of the teaching that Matthew gives as the Sermon on the Mount. Matthew's parable speaks of rock and sand (Matthew 7:24–27); Luke's builder digs deep to lay a foundation, and the danger is a river in flood. The image fits a land where dry stream beds can suddenly fill with water after heavy rain.
str: v. 46: the question: why call me “Lord” and not do what I say?
v. 47: the one who comes, hears and acts.
v. 48: like a man who dug deep and built on rock.
v. 49: the one who hears and does not act: a house without a foundation.
kw: The title of faith and worship. Jesus does not reject it; he asks that it be true in life as well as on the lips.
Solid bedrock under the soil. The rock is his word heard and done; behind it stands Jesus himself, the sure foundation.
vv: Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I tell you?
A gentle but searching question. Prayer and worship are not opposed to action; they are meant to lead into it.
That one is like a man building a house, who dug deeply and laid the foundation on rock;
Digging deeply takes time and effort and cannot be seen once the house stands. So it is with prayer, Scripture and the sacraments: the hidden work holds the visible life up.
But the one who hears and does not act is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation.
Both men heard the word. The difference is not knowledge but obedience. The storm does not create the difference; it reveals it.
ch: St James says the same: “be doers of the word, and not merely hearers who deceive themselves” (James 1:22). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the word of God is the support and energy of the Church, the food of the soul and the pure and lasting source of spiritual life (Dei Verbum 21). The house built on rock is the life that receives this word not only in the ear but in the hands.

qa: Does “nailing the record to the cross” mean that God's commandments no longer bind Christians?

No. What is nailed to the cross is the record of our debt, the sentence that stood against us, not God's holy will. Jesus himself said, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:17), and the Church teaches that the Ten Commandments bind Christians (CCC 2068). Grace does not abolish the commandments; it gives us the strength to keep them out of love.
study: Paul says that in Christ I have come to fullness. Where am I looking for fullness elsewhere?
What is one word of Jesus that I have heard many times but have not yet put into practice?
